name: Mach
baseline: unspecified C# HTTP server (probably ASP.NET Core; the repo file is only labelled 'csharp', server code not included)
workload: wrk against a trivial endpoint (204 no-content for 'plain'), 16 threads, 100 connections, 30 s, plus headers, cookies, body and JSON model-binding variants, run on loopback via benchmarks/runner/request_runner.py.
claimed_speedup: No faster-than claim is made; README says only 'designed to provide high HTTP throughput' and points to machframework.dev/benchmarks (EGRESS_BLOCKED, not opened). The repo's own CSVs at 16 threads / 100 connections give Mach 280385.96 req/s vs 100290.9 req/s for the 'csharp' file on plain (2.80x, derived from page data), 280097 vs 221091.36 headers (1.27x), 280342.45 vs 234736.06 cookies (1.19x), 156975.64 vs 101549.67 body (1.55x), 280337.85 vs 253793.28 small JSON binding (1.10x); Mach is slower on large JSON binding, 149575.36 vs 307173.48 (0.49x). Against the file labelled 'drogon' Mach is slower on every row: plain 280385.96 vs 1072586.17 req/s (Drogon 3.83x faster, derived from page data).
compiler_and_flags: Runner uses the CMake 'release' build directory (build/release/benchmarks/RequestBenchmarks); exact compiler and flags not stated.
tradeoffs: Built on Boost.Asio and Boost.Beast. v1.0 supports only Windows (MSVC) and Ubuntu (GCC). Very new, tiny user base (3 stars), 526 commits on main.
caveats: Weak and mixed evidence. (1) Mach publishes no claim of beating any named baseline; the only comparison data are two CSVs (request_wrk_results_csharp.csv and request_wrk_results_drogon.csv) with no server source, no versions, no hardware, no compiler flags. (2) The Mach rows (request_wrk_results.csv, commit de36047) and the comparison rows (commit 34c12a4) are from different runs on 2026-08-11 and may not share a machine or build. (3) Handler work in the comparison servers is unknown; Mach's 'plain' route returns 204 no content. (4) The 'csharp' win is cherry-picked in the sense that Mach loses on large JSON binding (0.49x), and Drogon, the C++ incumbent, is 1.6x to 6.8x faster than Mach on every row. (5) Website results page machframework.dev/benchmarks could not be opened (EGRESS_BLOCKED). Kept only because a numeric comparison against a named class of baseline exists; it is not evidence that Mach is faster than the C++ incumbent.

name: Muduo
baseline: libevent 2.x (libevent2) ping-pong echo server and client
workload: Ping-pong echo throughput benchmark (client and server both echo, as in the Boost.Asio LinuxPerformanceImprovements method) between muduo and libevent2 over loopback, varying message size and number of connections.
claimed_speedup: Author's blog post 'muduo vs libevent2 throughput' concludes muduo throughput is on average more than 18% higher than libevent2 (as quoted by the evpp benchmark page: 'muduo throughput averages more than 18% higher than libevent2').
compiler_and_flags: Not stated for the 18% claim (author's blog, not opened). The test code is public: chenshuo/recipes pingpong/libevent (Makefile CFLAGS -g -Wall -O2, single_thread.sh pins server and client with taskset) and chenshuo/muduo examples/pingpong (muduo built release via BUILD_TYPE=release ./build.sh).
tradeoffs: Linux-only (epoll, kernel >= 2.6.28), reactor-per-thread design, requires Boost only for boost::any. One-loop-per-thread model with its own Buffer class based on std::vector<char>.
caveats: The 18% figure comes from the author's 2010 CSDN blog post (blog.csdn.net/solstice/article/details/5864889, EGRESS_BLOCKED, not opened) and is seen only as quoted by the evpp project's benchmark page and a WebSearch snippet, so hardware, compiler and per-row numbers for muduo vs libevent2 are not verified here; tier C, first-party. The benchmark code for both sides is public in chenshuo/recipes/pingpong (libevent server.c and client.c, run scripts) but the exact build flags used for the published run are unknown. The evpp page's own muduo-v1.0.9 table (Xeon E5-2630 v2, CentOS 6.2, gcc 4.8.2) compares muduo with evpp, not libevent2, and shows them roughly equal. libevent version in the original post is a 2010-era 2.0.x. Last commit is 2025-02-28 (stale).

name: mongoose (Cesanta embedded web server)
baseline: lwIP (raw API) TCP/IP stack with its HTTP server
workload: HTTP requests per second served by an STM32 Nucleo-F746ZG over Ethernet to a workstation, Mongoose (built-in TCP/IP stack) vs lwIP raw integration; the same article also compares flash and RAM footprint.
claimed_speedup: Mongoose 1080 requests per second vs lwIP raw 286 requests per second (about 3.8x, derived from snippet); firmware size 28k with Mongoose vs 160k with lwIP raw (the same article says raw lwIP can be configured to use less RAM than Mongoose).
hardware: STM32 Nucleo-F746ZG (Cortex-M7) board on Ethernet, benchmark run from a workstation
tradeoffs: Dual licensed: GPL-2.0-only or paid commercial licence from Cesanta; embedded targets (STM32, NXP, ESP32, RP2040 and others) plus POSIX and Windows. Two-file C library (mongoose.c, mongoose.h) with built-in TCP/IP, HTTP, WebSocket, MQTT, TLS 1.3.
caveats: Vendor article: Cesanta sells Mongoose, so first-party; tier C. Numbers are snippet only: mongoose.ws is EGRESS_BLOCKED and the page was not opened, so test setup, compiler flags, lwIP configuration, payload size and whether lwIP used its own httpd are unverified. The README itself carries no benchmark; the project's repo contains no benchmark against nginx or any other HTTP server. Comparison is against an embedded TCP/IP stack on a microcontroller, not against a desktop HTTP server such as nginx.

name: nghttp2 (nghttpx HTTP/2 proxy)
baseline: Apache Traffic Server (ATS) as HTTP/2 terminating reverse proxy
workload: Yahoo engineer's HTTP/2 benchmarking of ATS vs nghttpx (h2load clients), both terminating HTTP/2 and proxying requests, 3 large image objects (60 KB to 200 KB) per connection, same number of threads, logs on, no OCSP stapling, no ATS cache; metric was server CPU utilization at the same traffic load.
claimed_speedup: Peak system CPU utilization under the same traffic load: ATS 18%, nghttpx 15%; idle process CPU ATS 0.5%, nghttpx 0%; idle system CPU ATS 7%, nghttpx 6.5%. No throughput or latency comparison seen.
stars_or_usage: 5.1k stars; libnghttp2 is the HTTP/2 backend of curl and many servers
tradeoffs: Evidence is for the nghttpx proxy application in the nghttp2 repo, not the libnghttp2 framing library. The library is a callback-based C API with no I/O of its own.
caveats: Very weak, snippet only: the PDF (Apache wiki, authored by Kit Chan of Yahoo, 2015, id 56066455) is EGRESS_BLOCKED on both cwiki hosts and was never opened; numbers come from a WebSearch snippet summary. Measures CPU utilization at fixed load, not requests per second or latency, so it is an efficiency result rather than a speed result. Hardware, versions and flags unknown. 2015-era ATS HTTP/2 implementation. The nghttp2 README's own h2load example (129658 req/s on localhost) is a tool demo with no comparison. Kept only because it is the sole numeric comparison found; confidence low.
